memory_candidates.content: When calibrating a corpus-wide zero-tolerance threshold (e.g. a control-character/NUL check), measure the REAL target corpus first, not just the motivating bad example. In the literature extension's corpus, ~half of all documents legitimately carry low-range Unicode Cc control codepoints (0x01-0x1F) as a benign glyph-substitute convention for math symbols under a broken/partial ToUnicode CMap -- a blanket zero-tolerance Cc check would fail roughly half the corpus. NUL (\x00) specifically remained safe as zero-tolerance (0 occurrences except one genuine already-ingested defect). The general lesson: split a proposed single check into 'genuinely always-zero-provenance' (zero-tolerance) vs. 'pervasive-but-usually-benign' (ratio/floor with calibrated headroom) based on an actual measurement sweep, not the first-draft wording of the check.

pymupdf4llm.to_markdown() applies its own heuristic character-substitution/cleanup pass beyond raw PyMuPDF (fitz) text extraction -- confirmed via page.get_text('dict'), which preserves literal control characters (e.g. embedded via page.insert_text()) intact, while to_markdown() on the same PDF silently alters them (digit swaps like '0'->'O', stray substitute glyphs). This means a synthetic PDF fixture built with insert_text() to simulate broken-font-encoding corruption may reproduce the defect on PyMuPDF's raw/fallback extraction path but NOT on pymupdf4llm's primary path, even though both ultimately read the same underlying PDF content stream. Useful to know before assuming a fixture that fails one extraction tier will fail both.
